analysis.one_liner: Bans organophosphate, neonicotinoid, and paraquat pesticides and strengthens farmworker and community protections.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 24 House Democrats behind it, never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the main federal pesticide law. It would immediately and permanently cancel the registrations of three classes of pesticides — organophosphates, neonicotinoids, and paraquat — and stop the sale of any remaining stocks. It would also force faster EPA review of pesticides the European Union or Canada has banned, cap conditional registrations at two years, require labels to list inert ingredients, let cities and counties adopt their own pesticide rules, and set up mandatory reporting of farmworker poisonings with penalties for employers who fail to report or retaliate.
analysis.who_benefits: Children, farmworkers, and rural residents exposed to pesticides linked to brain damage in children, Parkinson's disease, and cancer; communities that want local pesticide restrictions; and pollinators and endangered species affected by neonicotinoids and organophosphates.

how_it_helps.text: Immediately cancels the registration of all organophosphate pesticides, which scientists have repeatedly linked to neurodevelopmental damage in children, and revokes the food tolerances that allow their residues [S3].
Immediately cancels paraquat, exposure to which causes heart, kidney, and liver failure and greatly increases Parkinson's disease risk [S3].
Immediately cancels neonicotinoid pesticides, which the bill's findings link to the rapid decline of pollinators [S3].
Creates a citizen petition process to designate a pesticide as dangerous, with automatic suspension if the EPA misses deadlines, and lets any person sue the EPA to enforce it [S2][S3].

Requires pesticide labels to be printed in English and Spanish, mandates employer reporting of farmworker poisoning incidents to an online system with anonymous reporting, and imposes fines, criminal penalties, and $25,000 rewards to deter retaliation [S3].
Lets cities, counties, and other local governments adopt pesticide protections that state preemption currently blocks [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers lose the sales of entire product lines, and farmers lose access to these pest-control tools, with possible costs passed into food production.

drawbacks.text: The cancellations take effect immediately by operation of law, without the individual case-by-case scientific review and hearings the existing law provides, so pesticides in the same class could be banned together even where the evidence for a particular product is weaker [S3].

In deciding whether banned-abroad pesticides are dangerous, the EPA is explicitly prohibited from considering the economic costs to farmers of losing the product, which critics would call an incomplete analysis [S3].
Farmers could face higher costs or reduced crop protection, since some organophosphates and neonicotinoids are widely used in agriculture and replacements may be more expensive [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health stakes are large — the bill targets pesticide classes linked to childhood brain damage, Parkinson's disease, farmworker poisonings, and pollinator collapse, and the US still allows dozens of pesticides the EU has banned [S3]. The costs fall on specific manufacturers and on farmers who would need substitutes, and the bill's automatic, no-hearing cancellations and ban on weighing economic costs are blunt tools that skip the individualized review the current law requires [S3]. Weighing those honestly, the public health and farmworker protections are the dominant effect, but the design would invite legal challenges and disruption for growers.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Agriculture Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Neguse introduced the bill on August 4, 2020, joined by 23 Democratic cosponsors [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Agriculture Committee on the day of introduction [S5].
On September 11, 2020, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Biotechnology, Horticulture, and Research, and no further action was recorded [S5].
The committee never held a markup and the House never voted on the bill before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pesticide manufacturers keep selling organophosphates, neonicotinoids, and paraquat in the US, and the EPA's existing review process remains unchanged; farmworkers and communities seeking stronger protections gained nothing.

for.name: Joe Neguse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 23 cosponsors.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chair Rep. Collin Peterson (D-TX)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill, referring it to a subcommittee where it sat until the Congress ended.

against.name: Agricultural and pesticide industry
against.role: Pesticide registrants and farm groups opposing pesticide bans
against.what_they_did: Opposed bans on widely used pesticides; the Agriculture Committee, which oversees the industry's central law, took no action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 24 supporters — the sponsor and 23 cosponsors — were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Democratic chair of the Agriculture Committee never advanced it.

industries.note: The bill immediately and permanently cancels organophosphates, neonicotinoids, and paraquat, bans sale of existing stocks, and caps conditional registrations, eliminating major product lines [S3]. The industry's interest in keeping these products on the market runs directly against the health protections the bill offers the public [S3].

Farmers lose access to widely used pest-control tools, but the bill's ban on neonicotinoids responds to pollinator decline, which also threatens crop yields, and farmworker protections cover their workforce [S3].
Employers would face mandatory reporting of worker poisoning incidents, per-day fines for failures, criminal penalties for suppressing reports, and $25,000 whistleblower rewards [S3].
